# Autoimmune pancreatitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the pancreas > Autoimmune pancreatitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/p90LoR)

---

## Summary

Autoimmune <u>pancreatitis</u> (<u>AIP</u>) is a form of <u>chronic pancreatitis</u> that typically manifests with <u>obstructive jaundice</u> and mild epigastric <u>pain</u>. It is characterized by lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, <u>fibrosis</u>, and a strong response to <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy. There are two subtypes of <u>AIP</u>. <u>Type 1 AIP</u> is the <u>pancreatic</u> manifestation of systemic <u>IgG4-related disease</u>, typically affecting older men, and it is associated with other organ involvement. <u>Type 2 AIP</u> is a <u>pancreas</u>-specific disorder, often seen in younger individuals, with no sex predominance, and it is frequently associated with <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>, especially <u>ulcerative colitis</u>. The diagnosis is based on a combination of imaging findings (e.g., a sausage-shaped <u>pancreas</u>), serum IgG4 levels, <u>histology</u>, and response to <u>glucocorticoids</u>. The primary goal is to differentiate <u>AIP</u> from <u>pancreatic cancer</u>. Management for symptomatic patients involves inducing remission with <u>glucocorticoids</u>, followed by a tapering schedule. <u>Maintenance therapy</u> may be considered for <u>type 1 AIP</u> to prevent relapse.
